domains.title: Sacred Mountain of Japan
domains.subtitle: Volcano, Pilgrimage, and National Symbol
domains.lead: Fuji is more than a mountain. For over a thousand years it has been a volcano kami, a Buddhist mandala, and the defining image of Japan — a nearly perfect cone rising alone above the clouds, watched from every road. Pilgrims climb it, poets praise it, and artists have made its snow-capped form one of the most reproduced images on earth.

cards.name: Volcano Deity
cards.desc: As a living volcano, Fuji has been feared and worshipped as a source of both destruction and fertility.

cards.name: Pilgrimage Peak
cards.desc: For centuries pilgrims climbed to the summit, where shrines and lodges marked the path.

cards.name: National Symbol
cards.desc: Its image identifies Japan in art, currency, passports, and global imagination.

cards.name: Artistic Muse
cards.desc: Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views made Fuji an icon of world art.

symbols.name: Snow-capped cone
symbols.meaning: The visual form that has made Fuji a universal symbol of Japan — perfect geometry over restless fire

mythology.lead: Fuji generates story because it cannot be ignored: a volcano that sleeps for centuries at a time, a goddess of fire hidden under snow, and an image so constant that a whole civilization has measured its seasons, its festivals, and its art against one unchanging silhouette.

myths.title: The Name and Its Power
myths.text: Folk etymology explains the name as fushi, 'without equal,' or fuji, 'inexhaustible' — both appropriate to a mountain with no rival on the horizon. In the early chronicles the peak's deity was treated as female, a kami of fire, and in the medieval period she was identified with Sengen (Asama-no-kami) and with Konohanasakuya-hime, the blossom princess of the Kojiki, whose marriage to the heavenly grandson Ninigi bound heaven's line to the earth. When Fuji smoked or rumbled, the interpretation was immediate: the goddess of the volcano was stirring, and the province looked to its Sengen shrines. The shrine cult kept the mountain's divinity local and specific — not an abstraction like 'nature,' but a named power with festivals, priests, and a genealogy reaching back to the age of the gods. The mountain's own name became the nation's shorthand for what is highest, purest, and most alone.

myths.title: Fuji as Lotus Mandala
myths.text: In the medieval imagination Fuji was not climbed so much as entered. Buddhist exegetes mapped the mountain as a lotus mandala, its ridges the lotus petals, its crater the heart of the world; ascending it was circumambulation and pilgrimage at once. In the sixteenth century the ascetic Hasegawa Kakugyō is credited with founding the Fuji-kō confraternities, and by the Edo period tens of thousands of pilgrims climbed in white robes reciting sutras, carrying miniature shrines up the stations and building fujizuka — small replica Fujis — in the cities, so that those who could not travel could still 'climb' the mountain. Some confraternities worshipped the crater itself as the Pure Land. The practice reveals the mountain's genius as an image: Fuji is endlessly reproducible, and every reproduction is still Fuji — a mandala you can ascend with your feet, a paradise with a weather problem.

myths.title: The Floating World's Mountain
myths.text: Between about 1830 and 1850 the ukiyo-e masters fixed Fuji's image for the world. Hokusai's Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji placed the same snow-cap behind the Great Wave, a lumberyard, a tea-house balcony, a thunderstorm — proving the mountain was a measuring stick for every human activity. Hiroshige answered with travel series in which Fuji appears at a roadside halt, over a river, beyond a station bell. The prints used the newly imported Prussian blue so lavishly that the pigment itself became a fashion, and when Japan opened, these images were among the first things the West saw and imitated. The lesson of the series is visual relativism: Fuji never changes, but every viewpoint is a different picture. The mountain became the constant against which a whole floating world arranges and rearranges itself — and the proof that a sacred image, printed a hundred thousand times, loses none of its sanctity.

myths.title: The Last Eruption
myths.text: On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of 1707 — mid-December by the modern calendar — Fuji woke. The Hōei eruption blew ash downwind for weeks, darkening the sky over Edo itself, where official memoranda and ink paintings measured the fall in handspans and the city coughed through a winter of grey snow. The eruption opened vents on the southeastern flank and built the cinder cone still called Hōei-zan, but no lava flow reached the villages, and no death was recorded. Contemporaries read the smoke as the mountain kami's displeasure; modern seismologists read it as a warning clock — more than three centuries quiet, but the magma plumbing intact beneath a sacred cone. Either way the meaning is the same: Fuji is worshipped precisely because it is not safe — a goddess who sleeps with one eye open over forty million people, and whose last performance is remembered in ash that fell on the shogun's capital.

lore.syncretism: Fuji is a palimpsest of religious traditions. Shinto's Sengen shrines honor the mountain's volcanic kami — under the honji suijaku logic of the medieval centuries, a local kami read as the trace of a universal Buddha. Buddhist Fuji-kō confraternities climbed the mountain as a living mandala; Shugendō mountain ascetics used its slopes for training; and medieval exegetes mapped its ridges onto a lotus. The Meiji state, separating Shinto from Buddhism, promoted Fuji as a national emblem — the purest form of Japan itself — and the image followed the armies abroad and the recovery at home. After more than three centuries of dormancy, the 1707 Hōei eruption reminded the capital that the sacred mountain is still alive: the goddess under the snow has never signed a truce.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fuji was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2013 — 'Fujisan, sacred place and source of artistic inspiration' — and remains Japan's most photographed and climbed mountain, some three hundred thousand climbers each summer ascending through the night to greet the goraikō, the honored arrival of the sunrise. Its image sits on banknotes and passports and in a hundred million phone galleries; school songs still teach children that it is the noblest mountain in the world. The pilgrimage endures in secular costume — the white robes are rental gear now, the sutras are headlamps — but the shape of the act is unchanged: to reach the summit before dawn and watch the sun rise out of the Pacific, as pilgrims have done since the mountain was a goddess.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Fuji asks us to look at what endures. Cities rise and fall, governments change, but the mountain remains, altering only its cap of snow with the seasons. It is a natural fact that became a national dream.

Yet the dream works because the fact refuses to cooperate with it: Fuji is a volcano, not a monument, and its 1707 eruption fell ash on Edo like a reminder that the symbol can still act. That tension — perfect form over restless fire — is the mountain's real teaching. A culture that fixes its eye on one unchanging thing buys itself a measuring stick for everything that changes; and the thing it chooses had better be beautiful, because it will be looked at, in longing, for a thousand years. Fuji is.

lore.archaeology: Fuji is ringed by Sengen shrines, of which Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha in Fujinomiya — its present main hall a 1604 Tokugawa rebuilding — is the head of the cult. The 2013 World Heritage listing protects twenty-five component sites: Yamamiya and Murayama Sengen shrines on the old pilgrim approaches, the Yoshida and Subashiri trailheads with their station lodges and boundary markers, the lava tree-molds of Aokigahara's Sea of Trees, and the summit crater with its own Sengen sanctuary. The Hōei eruption of 1707 left a cinder cone on the flank and tephra beds as far as Edo, recorded in contemporary paintings and official memoranda. Every summer's climbers walk, step for step, a route fixed by the Fuji-kō confraternities four centuries ago.
